summary: Provides guidelines for authors and reviewers of standards-track specifications containing MIB modules. Parts may also be useful for reviewing other MIB documents. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4181 gives authors and reviewers shared rules for MIB documents. It covers both the document sections and the technical definitions used to describe managed network information.

subtitle: Guidelines for writing and reviewing IETF documents that contain MIB modules.

tldr.problem: Standards-track documents containing MIB modules need expert review, and reviewers need consistent guidance on documentation and SMIv2 usage.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4181 sets document requirements and gives technical guidance for names, data types, tables, notifications, compliance statements and revisions.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Best Current Practice 111. It has been updated by RFC 4841.

today: RFC 4181 is Best Current Practice 111, published in September 2005. It has been updated by RFC 4841.

sections.title: Why MIB Documents Need Review Guidelines
sections.content:
The IESG requires expert review of IETF standards-track specifications that contain Management Information Base (MIB) modules. Reviewers check documentation practices and whether modules meet the syntax and meaning rules of SMIv2.

This memo records the guidelines used in those reviews. It clarifies ambiguous requirements and updates recommendations where experience showed them to be suboptimal. Some guidance may also help authors of other MIB documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Experts review standards-track documents that define MIB modules. This memo explains what reviewers check so authors can prepare clear, consistent documents.

sections.title: Required Parts of a MIB Document
sections.content:
A MIB document must contain six parts: MIB boilerplate, narrative sections, definitions, Security Considerations, IANA Considerations and References. The overview must describe the module's scope and its relationship to other standards and modules.

The definitions must use SMIv2; SMIv1 is no longer acceptable in IETF MIB modules. The security section must identify sensitive or writable objects and explain their risks. The IANA section is required even when no IANA action is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Every MIB document needs the same main sections, including security, IANA and references. It must explain what the module covers and how it relates to other modules.

sections.title: Names, Identifiers and the Registration Tree
sections.content:
Standard module names must be unique and must not change when a module is revised. Descriptors and labels may exceed the recommended 32 characters for clarity, but they must not exceed 64 characters. The RFC recommends mnemonic module names.

Objects intended for operational use must not be registered under the experimental subtree. Standards-track modules should place their MODULE-IDENTITY under the mgmt subtree. The invocation must appear immediately after IMPORTS, and its object identifier must be unique.
sections.plainLanguage: Names and object identifiers let software refer to MIB definitions consistently. Authors should choose clear names and put operational objects in the correct registration tree.

sections.title: Choosing Data Types and Descriptions
sections.content:
Choose a data type that matches the information: INTEGER for enumerations, Integer32 for values that may be negative, Gauge32 for values that rise and fall, and Unsigned32 for non-negative values that do not decrease. Counter32 and Counter64 must follow counter semantics; they must not require a reset at a specified time or let a manager reset them.

A DESCRIPTION clause tells implementers how an object works, so it must be clear and unambiguous. For conceptual tables, use AUGMENTS for a one-to-one extension and INDEX for sparse relationships. Object identifiers have a limit of 128 sub-identifiers, which table indexes must respect.
sections.plainLanguage: Each value needs a type that matches how it behaves, such as a counter that does not decrease or a gauge that can move both ways. Clear descriptions help different implementations behave consistently.

sections.title: Notifications, Compliance and Revisions
sections.content:
A notification must identify the object instances it carries and explain their meaning. Its object identifier must have zero as its next-to-last sub-identifier. If events can arrive rapidly, the document must specify a way to limit notification rates.

Every accessible object must belong to an object group, every notification to a notification group, and every standard module must have a compliance statement. When revising a module, keep its name, existing definitions, descriptors and assigned object identifiers; changing them can break compatibility with deployed agents and importing modules.
sections.plainLanguage: Notifications need clear definitions and a limit when events can arrive rapidly. Revisions should preserve names and identifiers because other software may depend on them.

sections.title: Security, IANA and the Review Checklist
sections.content:
Deploying a MIB module can introduce security risks. Authors and reviewers must make sure those risks are disclosed using the approved security guidance. RFC 4181 itself describes what a MIB document's IANA section should contain but requests no registry change.

Appendix A provides a ten-item checklist covering draft boilerplate, abstract, MIB boilerplate, security, IANA, references, copyright, intellectual property, other document issues and technical content. It emphasizes reading the MIB from an implementer's point of view.
sections.plainLanguage: Every MIB document must explain security risks and state its IANA needs. The review checklist helps authors check both document requirements and technical clarity.
